messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert is a sixty-three-year-old married physician, a hospital internist who had always taken pride in his steady hand and calm demeanor under pressure. That changed five years ago on a Tuesday evening when he was riding the city bus home after a double shift. Two men boarded, shouting orders in clipped, furious voices: “Everyone down! Don’t move!” He dropped to the floor as gunfire erupted, his face pressed against the grimy rubber mat, smelling diesel and blood. He stayed frozen while screams and footsteps moved past him. He survived without physical injury, but the sound of those commands—the authority in the voices—etched itself into him.

In the months that followed, Robert found himself unable to shake the feeling that the world was fundamentally unsafe. His life, he came to believe, had been destroyed—not in a single moment, but slowly, as the confidence he had in people and in his own safety eroded. He started to distrust even familiar colleagues and neighbors, convinced that anyone could hide dangerous intentions. That distrust fed a constant vigilance: at home, he would lie awake listening for the creak of a floorboard or the click of a door latch, certain someone was entering. Even inside his own house he felt on guard, his muscles tight, his attention split. His wife noticed his irritability—sharp outbursts over small things, a new and unsettling edge to his voice.

Work became a minefield. Robert’s hospital, like any, ran on orders and instructions. A senior physician telling him to review a chart, a nurse relaying a protocol change—each command, however routine, triggered a visceral replay of the bus. In those moments, his old belief that the world was a dangerous place felt freshly confirmed, and his distrust of others deepened. That distrust, in turn, made him more alert to authority figures, so he began to notice commands everywhere, anticipating them as threats. The bus itself he simply stopped using; he drove or took expensive taxis, which strained the family budget and added to his wife’s quiet frustration.

The cycle tightened. Every hypervigilant scan of his home—listening for sounds of an intruder—fed his conviction that danger was imminent and that his old life was irretrievable. That conviction, in turn, kept his guard up, so he never felt safe enough to let down his monitoring. He became short-tempered at the hospital, snapping when flustered, and his colleagues learned to give him wide berth. His wife told him she felt she was living with a stranger. A few weeks ago, after a particularly harsh argument about a forgotten errand, she said she could not keep going this way. That was what finally brought Robert to my office.

He sits across from me now, still watchful, his hands resting on his knees. He says he is tired of being afraid in his own home, tired of the anger that surges without warning. He hopes therapy can help him reclaim some of the steadiness he lost on that bus floor. But underneath that hope, what frightens him most is the suspicion that the damage might be permanent—that his life really has been destroyed, and that no amount of talking will put it back together.
